beats.intro: Lesson seventeen. [[sub]]Why one person often needs two bosses, and what it takes to make that work.
beats.nasa: To put a man on the moon, NASA had several major contractors, and many subcontractors, each working on a different part. [[units]]Every team answered to its own company. [[pm]]But a project manager from outside, from NASA, had as much say over their work as the company's own management. [[shift]]So when one team slipped, resources could move from a strong team to help it catch up, and the whole schedule held. [[matrix]]The approach became known as matrix management. Grove calls it dual reporting on a grand scale. [[old]]But the idea was not new. It had quietly kept hybrid organizations running for years: the neighbourhood high school, Alfred Sloan's General Motors, even the breakfast factory, once it franchised.
beats.security: Intel stumbled onto dual reporting when it was young and small. The question at a staff meeting: who should the security officers at the new outlying plants report to? [[pm]]Choice one, the plant manager. He is there every day. [[pmbad]]But he is usually an engineer or a manufacturing person, who knows little about security, and cares even less. [[sm]]Choice two, the corporate security manager. He hired them, and he sets the standards they must follow. [[smbad]]But he works at headquarters. How would he know if they even showed up, or came in late? He wouldn't. [[both]]So, report to both. [[how]]The security manager says how the job should be done. [[watch]]The plant manager watches how it is done, day by day.
beats.boss: The answer solved both problems, but the staff couldn't quite accept it. [[q]]A person has to have a boss, they said. So who is in charge here? [[two]]Can someone really have two bosses? [[yes]]The answer was a tentative yes. [[birth]]And so Intel's culture of dual reporting was born. Grove says it was a slow, laborious birth.
beats.career: Yet the need for it is fundamental. Think about how a manager comes to be. [[s1]]He starts as an individual contributor, say a salesperson. [[s2]]He does well, and becomes a sales manager, supervising other salespeople. [[s3]]He is promoted again, to regional sales manager. At Intel, he now also manages field application engineers, who know far more about technical matters than he does. [[s4]]In time he becomes general manager of a whole division, including manufacturing, which he has never done. [[gen]]He can supervise his manufacturing manager on the general side of the job. The technical side he has to leave alone. [[other]]Elsewhere, manufacturing managers report to people who rose through engineering, or finance.
beats.fix: One fix: name a senior manufacturing manager, and have every manufacturing manager report to him instead. [[func]]But the more you do that, the closer you get to a purely functional organization. [[lose]]The general manager could no longer pull finance, marketing, engineering and manufacturing together toward one business purpose that answers the market. [[both]]Grove wants both. [[gm]]The urgency and the operating priorities, from the general manager. [[tech]]And a technical supervisor, for how the work is done. [[dual]]The solution is dual reporting.
beats.peers: Does the technical supervisor have to be one person? No. [[cafe]]Picture a manufacturing manager having coffee in the cafeteria. A manufacturing manager from another division comes over. His general manager came up through finance. [[share]]Chatting, they find they have technical problems in common. Two heads are better than one, [[often]]so they meet a bit more often. [[reg]]Then regularly. Managers from other divisions join. [[council]]Soon there is a council of peers, tackling the issues common to all. [[gives]]It gives them the supervision a general manager who knew manufacturing could have given. [[two]]Each manufacturing manager now reports to two supervisors: their general manager, and the group of peers.
beats.trust: To make such a group work, its members must give something up: the freedom to decide alone. [[vac]]Grove's analogy: two couples take a vacation together. [[less]]You know you won't be free to do exactly what you want, when you want. [[more]]You go anyway, because you'll have more fun. [[work]]At work, you go along with your peers' decisions in most cases. [[trust]]That depends on trusting the soundness of what the group decides. [[culture]]And trust is not an organizational principle. It is part of the culture: shared values and beliefs, and knowing how things are done here. A strong, positive culture is essential for dual reporting and peer decisions to work.
beats.ambig: This system makes a manager's life ambiguous, and most people dislike ambiguity. [[func]]But look at the simpler forms. A purely functional organization is clear on paper, but it cuts engineering and manufacturing off from the market. They lose sight of what customers want. [[miss]]A purely mission-oriented one has crisp reporting lines and clear objectives. But it fragments the company, and the result is inefficiency and poor performance. [[tried]]Intel tried everything else. The other models were less ambiguous. They just didn't work. [[demo]]Grove compares it to democracy: not great in itself, just the best way there is to organize.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Dual reporting gives one job two bosses, and it is old and widespread. [[w2]]The expert sets how the work is done; the local boss sees it done day by day. [[w3]]The technical boss can be a group of peers. [[w4]]Peer groups need members to give up some freedom, and that rests on trust and culture. [[w5]]It is ambiguous, but the simpler forms fail. Now the lesson practice.
